chunk-001:c004.proposition: Free will requires multiple genuinely possible alternatives and control by the person over which alternative becomes actual.

chunk-001:c007.proposition: Hard determinism is self-defeating because deliberating, arguing, and rationally accepting it invoke norms and alternatives that the doctrine denies.

chunk-001:c010.proposition: Evidence of external influences on behavior does not establish complete determination, particularly when the examples concern impairment rather than ordinary reason-responsive decisions.

chunk-002:c002-01.proposition: Under determinism, change occurs only when it is itself determined, leaving agents without control over whether change happens.

chunk-002:c002-03.proposition: Deterrence and incapacitation alone cannot explain why framing an innocent ex-convict is wrong while punishing the actual offender is permissible.

chunk-002:c002-05.proposition: A secret one-off framing remains unjust even when systemic consequences are excluded, leaving desert and retributive reasoning to explain the moral distinction.

chunk-002:c002-07.proposition: Past errors about responsibility do not warrant general skepticism about present beliefs unless those errors share a substantive premise with the belief now disputed.

chunk-002:c002-09.proposition: Without decisive scientific proof either way, the appearance of possessing free will provides a rational default until compelling contrary evidence emerges.

chunk-003:c003-01.proposition: An agent's reasons can explain a free choice even if there is no further determining explanation of why one reason prevailed over competing reasons.

chunk-003:c003-10.proposition: A microphysical determinism in which electrical and chemical brain events determine belief does not explain responsiveness to truth or epistemic reasons.
